newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault truck sales dip, fights to prop car sales.
newsitem.headline: Renault truck sales dip, fights to prop car sales.

text.p: French carmaker Renault revealed on Friday its loss on declining truck sales would be bigger than expected, but car sales were still rising, even if they seemed to be at the cost of serious discounting.
The group said car sales in the third quarter rose 5.33 percent to 33.329 billion francs ($6.55 billion), but sales slid 10.1 percent in the commercial vehicles division to 6.358 billion francs.
Stock market traders said the figures were better than they had expected and car industry analysts took much the same view.
They said, however, there were signs of severe price cutting because the rise in car sales revenue was small when compared with the increase in car registrations in the same period.

"It's a wonderful business -- giving away cars," commented one car industry analyst, pointing out that Renault was nevertheless far from alone in trying to secure sales in a stagnant European car market.
While the car sales raised few eyebrows, Renault said the previously predicted loss at its truck division in 1996 would now be worse than expected.
"The negative contribution from the commercial vehicles division will be considerably more pronounced than anticipated." it said in a statement on third quarter and nine-month sales.
"The Commercial Vehicles Division will have to cope with depressed markets in both Europe and the United States.

The efforts initiated in the area of cost reductions will not suffice to offset the negative influences of a difficult pricing environment and transition phase in the product line, with the launch of the Premium, as well as changes to emission standards in Europe."

Operating profit from trucks shrivelled to 26 million francs in the first half of 1996 from 519 million a year earlier. The far larger car division, stuck in the red since the second half of 1995, ran up a loss of 911 million francs in the first half.

Chairman Louis Schweitzer said in a recent interview in Le Monde he expected to end the year in the red, given the market outlook. Total profit for the group shrank to 158 million francs in the first six months from 1.76 billion francs previously.

The market took the latest figures largely in its stride and Renault's share rose in a generally stronger Paris stock market. The stock rose as much as 2.5 percent but slipped back with the market to stand 2.41 percent up at 123 francs at 1230 GMT, when the CAC 40 leading share index was up 0.98 percent.
"They are poor but not dramatic," one analyst said.
"On the car side, sales were up 5.33 percent but there's nothing good about that because registrations rose 21 percent in the quarter. "That means there's huge price discounting".
BZW analyst Philip Ayton said the market understood there was a trade-off between internal mesures to overhaul the group and the problems in the market generally.
"There's very little money being made by carmakers. Renault is facing up to the problem but it remains to be seen if it will be enough," he added.
Both Renault and rival French carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen said earlier this week they were talking to the government for help in restructuring their ageing workforces.
They have been reported by newspapers to be looking to shed 40,000 through early retirement while recruiting 14,000 younger staff.
The member of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's staff said on Friday the request was being examined but that no decision had been taken.
One newspaper put the estimated cost of the plan at 30 billion francs but neither company has confirmed any numbers. ($1=5.088 French Franc)
